name: Americas Mailbox — SD Mail & Domicile
description: This is my home base on paper. Americas Mailbox in Box Elder gives full-time travelers a real South Dakota address — for your driver's license, vehicle registration, voting, and mail forwarding — so you can be "from" a no-income-tax state while you roam the country. It's how I stay legal and reachable from anywhere. If you sign up, tell them mailbox #21195 referred you. (Their FAQ explains how it all works.)

name: NOCO Boost X GBX75 Jump Starter
description: 2,500 amps of "you're not stranded today" in something the size of a lunchbox. It'll jump the Sprinter's diesel, charge a phone as a power bank, and the built-in light has bailed me out of more than one dark-campsite fix. The piece of gear I hope I never need — and am very glad I have.

name: Koonie 10,000mAh Clip-On Camping Fan + Lantern
description: A still, hot night in the van is the enemy of good sleep — and this little clip fan is the fix. Genuinely quiet, 360° tilt, runs all night on a charge, and doubles as a soft lantern. Clips to the bed frame, a cabinet, wherever you need the air. Small thing, huge difference.

name: The Bug Wall — Magnetic Bug Screens
description: On a summer evening the van doors want to be wide open — and every mosquito in the county knows it. The Bug Wall is the answer: magnetic screens handmade in the USA from marine canvas and no-see-um netting, cut to fit the Sprinter's sliding and rear door openings. No drilling — they hold on with magnets, part in the middle so you can walk through, and roll up out of the way when bug season ends. The breeze comes in, the bugs stay out, and the doors stay open into the night.

name: SOUDFK Rechargeable Bottle Lamp
description: Pop it on an empty wine bottle and the whole van goes warm and golden. Rechargeable, a few color tones, no cords — just soft light for the quiet end of a long road day. The little luxuries are what make a small space feel like home.

name: Camco Bamboo Folding Camp Table
description: Sets up in seconds, folds flat to nothing, and the bamboo top is sturdy enough to actually cook on. Camp coffee at sunrise, dinner prep, a hand of cards after dark — this little table is where a lot of the day ends up happening.

name: DALUOBO Removable RV Table Leg
description: The trick to living small: a table that disappears. This aluminum pedestal drops in when you need a surface and lifts right out when you don't — 360° rotation, adjustable height, no tools. Floor space back in two seconds.

name: TeamObsidian Waterproof Bike Cover
description: Bikes live on the back of the van through sun, rain, and highway grit — this heavy ripstop cover keeps the weather and road off them. Reflective straps, grab handles, and it cinches down tight so it won't flap at 70. Cheap insurance for gear that isn't.

name: The MILEPOST — Alaska Travel Planner
description: If you're pointing the rig north, this is the bible. Mile-by-mile logs of every highway through Alaska, the Yukon, and BC — every pullout, fuel stop, and view worth stopping for. Published since 1949, and still the one book I wouldn't drive the North Country without.

name: Neso Gigante Portable Sun Shade
description: Shade is the difference between a good camp afternoon and a miserable one. This throws 11 feet of UPF 50+ cover, anchors with sand bags instead of stakes (so it grips any ground), shrugs off wind, and packs to a shoulder bag. Beach, desert, dry lakebed — instant shade anywhere.

name: Milwaukee M18 Cordless Tire Inflator
description: Set the pressure, walk away — it stops on its own. Tops off the van tires, the bikes, an air mattress, whatever, all off the same M18 batteries as the rest of my tools. No more gas-station air-machine roulette. (Tool only — runs on M18 packs.)

name: LIHAN 12V Socket Splitter + USB
description: One cigarette socket is never enough in a van. This turns it into three switched 12V outlets plus USB-A and USB-C, with a voltmeter so you can keep an eye on the house battery at a glance. The little hub that ends up powering half the rig.

name: Gazelle T4 Overland Pop-Up Tent
description: Pops up in under a minute — no pole-threading, no swearing in the dark. A proper standing-room hub tent built tough enough for overlanding, for when I want to sleep outside the van or set up a basecamp. Up fast, down fast, solid in between.

name: Gazelle G6 Pop-Up Screen Gazebo
description: A bug-free room with a view. This six-sided screen house pops up in seconds and turns any campsite into a shaded, mosquito-proof hangout — eat, work, play cards, all without donating blood to the local bugs. Camp comfort, instantly.

name: Gazelle Gazebo Wind/Privacy Panels (3-Pack)
description: The upgrade that turns the G6 gazebo into a real shelter. These panels hook onto the open sides to block wind, rain, and prying eyes — a cozy, weatherproof room when the conditions (or the neighbors) call for it. (Panels only — fits the Gazelle gazebos.)

name: G4Free Folding Camp Chair
description: A real chair that packs down to almost nothing. High back, light frame, steady on uneven ground — the seat I actually want at the end of a long day, not the wobbly afterthought. Folds small enough to bring anywhere.

name: RIO Hammock Chair
description: The one I reach for at the end of the day. Reclines into a proper hammock-style cradle, packs into its own bag, and sets up anywhere there's a patch of ground and a sunset worth watching. Camp luxury that earns its space.

name: Starlink Mini 12V Car Power Adapter
description: The cable that lets the Starlink Mini run straight off the van's 12V — no inverter, no juggling power bricks. Weatherproof connector so it lives outside happily. This little adapter is what makes mobile Starlink actually mobile.

name: Starlink Mini — Satellite Internet
description: Internet from the actual middle of nowhere. The Starlink Mini is how I stay online out here — working, streaming, posting these very pages — when the nearest cell tower is an hour of dirt road away. The single biggest game-changer for life on the road. (My Starlink referral link — sign up through it and we may both earn Starlink credit.)

name: Bluetti Elite 300 Power Station
description: Three kilowatt-hours of quiet, off-grid power you can carry. Enough to run a fridge, an induction burner, tools, and every device for days between charges — and it tops back up fast off solar or shore power. This is camping free, off-grid, with none of the compromises.

name: Power Watchdog 30A RV Surge Protector
description: The bulldog that stands between my rig and whatever a sketchy campground pedestal is throwing out. It reads the power before it ever reaches the van — surges, high or low voltage, a miswired post — and cuts it off instantly if anything looks dangerous (that’s the EPO), then restores it once it’s safe. The Bluetooth app shows live voltage, amps, and watts right on my phone, and it shrugs off rain (IP65). One bad pedestal can fry thousands of dollars of electronics; this is the cheapest insurance in the rig. I plug in the Watchdog before I plug in anything else.

name: Midland X-TALKER T71VP3 Walkie-Talkies (Pair)
description: The peacemaker of the campground: hand one to your spotter and backing into a tight site becomes a calm conversation instead of a shouting match. Long-range FRS radios with 36 channels, privacy codes, and NOAA weather scan — no license needed — and they earn their keep again on trail hikes and caravan days when there’s no cell signal to be found.

name: Sawyer MINI Water Filter
description: Weighs almost nothing, costs almost nothing, and turns up to 100,000 gallons of sketchy water into safe drinking water. Stream, spigot, or a questionable campground tap — drink without the worry. The cheapest peace of mind I carry.

name: Pebblebee Rechargeable Tracker
description: Stick one on anything you can't afford to lose — keys, the camera bag, the drone case — and never tear the van apart looking again. Rechargeable (no battery-swap landfill), loud enough to find in a cluttered rig, and works with both Apple and Google Find My. Peace of mind for forgetful days.

name: KOSMEGAL Electric Air Pump
description: Inflates and deflates the paddleboard, the kayak, air mattresses, the lot — set the pressure and walk away. Runs off 12V, comes with every nozzle you'll need, and saves your lungs and your back. Turns "let's blow up the SUP" from a chore into a two-minute job.

name: ROC Inflatable Paddleboard (SUP)
description: Rolls up to backpack size, inflates rock-hard, and turns any lake, river, or quiet cove into the morning's adventure. Comes complete — paddle, pump, leash, bag — so there's no excuse not to get on the water. The best kind of "let's just see what's around that bend."

name: Anker Prime 160W GaN Charger
description: One tiny brick that fast-charges the laptop, phone, and tablet all at once — 160W across three ports, smaller than a deck of cards. It replaced the tangle of chargers I used to travel with, and the little smart display shows exactly what each port is pulling. Desk power, distilled.

name: ROÉKO 12V Socket Splitter (Corded)
description: A simple, fused 1-to-2 cigarette-lighter splitter on a short cord — the one I run to reach the back of the rig, or to tuck a dashcam and a fridge onto a single outlet. On/off switch, real 15A fuses, no fuss. The unglamorous bit of wiring that quietly powers everything.

name: The Hidden Life of Trees (Peter Wohlleben)
description: Read this one under a tree and you'll never walk through a forest the same way again. Wohlleben shows how trees talk, share, and remember — the secret social world beneath the canopy. The kind of book that makes the quiet places I love feel even more alive.

name: Solar TPMS Tire-Pressure Monitor (6-Sensor)
description: A blowout at highway speed in a heavy rig is the nightmare you can actually prevent. This watches every tire's pressure and temperature in real time and warns you before a slow leak becomes a roadside disaster. Solar-powered, sits on the dash, with sensors for every wheel — the van and a trailer if you tow one. Cheap insurance against the worst day on the road.

name: Beech Lane Curved RV Levelers
description: Pull up on uneven ground, drive a wheel up the curve until the bubble's centered, chock it, done — no stacking blocks, no guesswork. The difference between a fridge that runs right and a night spent sleeping on a slant. One of those "why didn't I buy these sooner" tools.

name: ODSD Portable Camping Stove & Grill
description: Griddle on one side, burner on the other — bacon and eggs at sunrise without leaving camp. Folds into its own case, shrugs off the wind with the built-in screens, and runs on propane. Real cooking, anywhere the view's worth stopping for.

name: Newentor Wireless Weather Station
description: Indoor and outdoor temp and humidity at a glance, plus a forecast — so I know whether tonight calls for the fan or the extra blanket, and whether tomorrow's a hiking day or a hunker-down day. The remote sensors let me watch the van's temperature from outside, too. Small comfort, big peace of mind.

name: Hard Carry Case for Starlink Mini
description: The Mini goes everywhere with me, so it rides in this — a waterproof, foam-fitted hard case that keeps the dish, router, and cables safe from dust, drops, and the general chaos of a moving van. Cheap protection for an expensive lifeline.

name: Starlink Mini Protective Cover
description: A fitted cover that shields the Mini's antenna from sun, rain, and grit while it's set up outside — keeps my lifeline working and looking new. The little add-on that protects the expensive bit.

name: USB-C to DC Power Adapter (PD 20V)
description: The little trick that lets the Starlink Mini (and other DC-barrel gear) run off a USB-C PD power bank or laptop charger instead of a fixed supply. Plug it inline and the Mini sips power from anything that can push 20V over USB-C. Tiny part, big flexibility for off-grid internet.

name: Finding Camp
description: The apps that find free, legal places to park. I lean on these constantly — see the toolkit in my guide.
